evidence: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five were reluctant to record 'The Message', judging it wrong for clubs, and Sylvia Robinson pushed it through and persuaded Melle Mel to write verses for it. Mel has said he took part without much enthusiasm at first. The episode is described consistently in oral histories of the record. Held at consensus because no first-hand source is named here (Q22).

later.title: The Message

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Listen to the tempo and then imagine a dancefloor. It does not work, and the group knew it did not work, which is why they did not want it. What the record buys with that refusal is room: at this speed a voice has time to finish a thought. Nearly everything rap does with slow tempo afterwards depends on somebody proving a slow rap record could sell.

explanation: Flash and the Furious Five made party music and 'The Message' was not party music: too slow, too bleak, no use in a club. They did not want to do it, and on their own terms they had a sound professional reason. Sylvia Robinson, who ran Sugar Hill, pushed it anyway and got Melle Mel to write verses; Mel has said he was not keen at first. It became the most important record any of them made, and afterwards rap could be about anything. It is an uncomfortable connection: the judgement that widened what rap could be about came from a label owner overruling the artists. It crosses lineages because Robinson's home was R&B and funk, not hip-hop, and that is the point of the story: the person who saw what rap could carry had spent twenty years in another business.
